newsitem.title: USA: American Air's pilots union shows signs of division.
newsitem.headline: American Air's pilots union shows signs of division.

text.p: The leader of a local branch of the union representing American Airlines pilots was quoted Thursday as criticising the union's handling of bitter contract negotiations with management.

Jay Courtney, chairman of the union's Dallas-Fort Worth area branch, said he believed an agreement could have been reached at negotiations last week and called on national leaders to give rank-and-file members another vote before authorising a possible strike in mid-April.
"The membership is crying out that they'd like to have another strike ballot," Courtney told The Dallas Morning News. "It is unfortunate that in the midst of all this, we cannot survey our pilots."
Courtney is one of the Allied Pilots Association's (APA) key local leaders. The Dallas-Fort Worth base has 2,800 pilots, about 30 percent of the union's nationwide membership.

Union leaders are resisting calls from some pilots for a strike vote. National President James Sovich attended a meeting of 650 pilots in Dallas on Wednesday but was less optimistic than Courtney on the chances of reaching a deal with the airline on a contract.

Sovich said a mid-April strike was "more probable than not" and that the two sides were still very far apart, especially on the issue of how to deploy a new breed of 50-seat and 70-seat regional jets.

American Airlines, a unit of Fort Worth-based AMR Corp., wants to give the jets to its low-cost commuter carrier American Eagle, which employs pilots from another union. But the Allied Pilots union accuses management of trying to "outsource" its members' jobs and insists that only American Airlines pilots be allowed to fly the jets.

Sovich flatly rejected recent newspaper reports that the union decided to back down on the regional jets issue during last week's failed negotiations. He accused the airline of leaking false reports to confuse union members.
"If that is the way they are going to stumble into a second strike, that is exactly what will happen," Sovich said.
American's 9,300 pilots went on strike at midnight last Friday but President Bill Clinton intervened minutes later, appointing a presidential board to help resolve the dispute.
The move forced the pilots to return to work and pushed back any strike by 60 days. Both sides are to put their case before the presidential board starting next week.

Sovich said the union was sticking to its demands on wages and regional jets, and that he firmly opposed any new strike ballot. Initial rank-and-file support for the first strike came with a January vote in which pilots rejected a tentative contract agreement by a 61-39 margin.

Union spokesman Gregg Overman said the union remains strong and that the leadership has full support of a vast majority of its members despite some concerns over strategy and the issue of a strike ballot.
"This is a democratic organisation so you are always going to have differences of opinion," Overman said. "Sometimes it's like making sausages: It's not pretty, but it works."
